author: bernard-of-clairvaux
fields.title: On Loving God
fields.subtitle: De Diligendo Deo
fields.description: On Loving God is Bernard of Clairvaux's great little treatise on why and how we should love God. Writing in the twelfth century, Bernard answers that we love God because of who He is and all He has given — and he traces the soul's ascent through four degrees of love, from loving self, to loving God for our own sake, to loving God for God's sake, and at last to loving even ourselves for God alone. Tender, searching, and short, it has fed the devotion of Christians for eight hundred years.
fields.attribution: Translated by Marianne Caroline and Coventry Patmore (London, 1884). Public domain.

fields.title: Why We Ought to Love God
fields.body_html:
You want me to explain why we should love God, and how much.

My answer is that God Himself is the reason we love Him, and that the right measure of that love is to love without measure. Is that clear enough? Perhaps it is for a thoughtful reader, but I want to answer for the learned and the unlearned alike. I may have said enough for the first, but I must remember the others too. For their sake I will open up what I mean, and perhaps add a little to it.

Two things move us to love God for His own sake: nothing is more reasonable, and nothing is more rewarding.

The question “Why should we love God?” can mean two things. It can mean “What right does He have to our love?” or it can mean “What good will it do us to love Him?” To both questions there is only one answer: the reason for loving God is God. No claim could be stronger than this. God gave Himself to us even though we were unworthy, and since He is God, what could He give us that is worth more than Himself? So if, when we ask why we must love God, we mean “What is His claim on us?”, the answer is above all this: He loved us first. That gives Him a right to be loved in return, especially when we consider who it is that loves, who it is He loves, and how He loves them. For who is it that loves us? It is the One to whom every spirit bears witness: “Thou art my God, Thou hast no need of my goods.” And is His love not that charity which does not seek its own interests? But on whom is this unselfish love set? The Apostle answers: “When we were yet enemies, we were reconciled to God.” God loved us with no thought of gain for Himself, and He loved us while we were still His enemies. And how did He love us? St. John puts it at its highest: “God so loved the world as to give His only begotten Son.” St. Paul adds: “He hath not spared His only begotten Son, but hath delivered Him up for us;” and the Son says of Himself, “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.” These are the claims that the holy God, supremely great and almighty, has on the love of small, weak and sinful human beings. Someone may say, “Yes, that is true of people, but not of angels.” I know. The angels did not need the same rescue. Yet the One who helped us in our misery also kept the angels from falling into misery like ours. If God’s love found a way of escape for us, it was that same love that kept the angels from a fall like ours.

fields.title: God's Right to Our Love
fields.body_html:
ANYONE who accepts what I have said must surely admit that we are bound to love God. But if there are unbelievers who will not admit even that much, God has enough to put their ingratitude to shame in the countless good things He gives to body and soul. Is it not from Him that we receive the bread that keeps us alive, the light we see by, and the air we breathe? I mention these first not because they are the greatest, since they concern only the body, but because they are the most necessary. For our greatest gifts we must look into the soul, the higher part of our being. Those gifts are dignity, understanding and virtue. By human dignity I mean our free will, which raises us above every other living creature and gives us rule over them. Understanding shows us this dignity, and at the same time shows us that we do not owe it to ourselves. And virtue makes us search eagerly for the One who made us, and, once we have found Him, hold on to Him with all our strength. Each of these three gifts has two sides. Dignity is the special privilege of human nature, and it is also the reason every other living creature has always feared us. Understanding sees our dignity, but also admits that although it is in us, it does not come from us. And virtue works in two ways: it drives us to seek eagerly the One to whom we owe our existence, and, when we find Him, to cling to Him just as eagerly. Dignity without understanding is worthless, and understanding without virtue can only do harm, as the following reasoning shows. No mind can take pride in what it is unless it knows what it is. But if it knows what it is and forgets that it did not make itself, but was made by Another, and so glories in itself and not in God, it should consider the Apostle’s words: “What hast thou that thou hast not received? Why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it?” He does not simply say, “Why dost thou glory?” He adds, “as if thou hadst not received it.” This shows that the fault is not in glorying that we have a gift, but in glorying as though we had not been given it. Such glorying is rightly called vainglory, because it does not stand on the solid rock of truth. The Apostle marks it off from true glory when he says: “He that glorieth may glory in the Lord,” that is, in the truth, for God is truth.

So there are two things we need to know: first, what we are; and second, that we did not make ourselves what we are. If we miss either one, we will either take no glory at all, or the glory we take for ourselves will be “vain.” And finally: “If thou know not thyself, go forth and wander after the flocks of thy companions.” This is exactly what happens. When a person held in honour does not know his own dignity, he is rightly compared, because of that ignorance, to the animals that share with him the decay and short life of this world. Not knowing itself, the creature that reason sets apart from the beasts mixes itself up with them. Because it does not know its own glory, which is all within, it gives itself to idle curiosity and busies itself with outward beauty that the senses can see. It sinks to the level of lower creatures because it does not know that it has been given something greater than they have. This is an ignorance we must carefully guard against. We must never think of ourselves as less than God has made us. But we must take even greater care to avoid the opposite ignorance, which makes us credit ourselves with more than we have. We do this when we wrongly imagine that the gifts we are aware of come from ourselves. Worse than either kind of ignorance, and to be hated and fled from even more, is the presumption that knowingly takes pride in the good we have, with no fear of robbing Another of the glory that belongs to Him for things we know perfectly well did not come from us. In the first case, we take no glory at all. In the second, we take glory, but not in God. In the third, we no longer sin in ignorance but on purpose, by seizing what belongs to God alone. This boldness is worse than the second fault, because it despises God, while the other simply did not know Him. Compared with the first, it makes us like devils, while the other only made us like beasts. Only pride, the greatest of all evils, can make us use the gifts we have received as if they were ours by nature, and rob our Benefactor, for our own benefit, of the glory that is rightly His. So to dignity and understanding we must add virtue, which is their proper fruit. It is by virtue that we seek and reach the generous Author of all things, the One to whom we should give in everything the glory that belongs to Him. Otherwise we will suffer for having known what was right and failed to do it.

Whoever does that has not used his understanding for good, but “hath devised iniquity on his bed.” Like a wicked servant, he has tried to divert and keep for himself the glory his good Master should have received, though his understanding told him plainly that he had no claim to it. It is clear, then, that dignity without understanding is useless, and that understanding without virtue leads to ruin. But for the one who has virtue, neither understanding nor dignity can do any harm. He lifts up his voice and eagerly praises God, saying: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but to Thy name be the glory;” which is to say: “Lord, we claim no understanding or dignity of our own. We give it all back to You, for everything we have comes from You.”

But we are wandering a little in our wish to prove that even those who do not know Christ are taught well enough by the natural law, and by the gifts of body and soul they have, to love God for His own sake. To repeat briefly what was said above: what unbeliever does not know that he has received everything he needs for life, light, air and food, from the One alone who makes His sun shine on the just and the unjust, and sends rain on saints and sinners? What person, however godless, credits the dignity peculiar to the human race to anyone except the One who says in Genesis, “Let us make man to Our Own image and likeness”? Who sees the author of understanding in anyone but the One who teaches all people? From whose hand would anyone expect to receive virtue, except from the God of virtue? So God has every right to be loved for His own sake, even by the reckoning of the unbeliever who does not know Christ. And whoever does not love the Lord his God with all his heart and soul and strength has no excuse, for his own inborn sense of justice and reason cries out from the depths of his soul that he is bound to love completely the One from whom he has everything. But it is very hard, in fact impossible, by natural strength or the power of free will alone, to give everything back to God instead of keeping some of it for our own praise. As it is written: “All seek their own;” and again: “The imagination and thought of man’s heart are prone to evil from his youth.”

fields.title: The Christian's Greater Motive to Love
fields.body_html:
BELIEVERS know very well how much they need Jesus crucified. Yet while they confess and wonder at His love, they feel no embarrassment that they have so little, nothing but themselves, to give back for a love so humble and so great. Their own love is stirred by knowing that they are loved so much and so freely, for the one who is loved little, loves little. Neither Jews nor pagans feel the wound of love as the Church does when she says: “Stay me up with flowers, compass me about with fruits: because I languish with love.” She sees Solomon wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him. She sees the only Son of the Father staggering under the weight of the cross; the God of all majesty bruised by blows and covered in spit; the Author of life and glory fastened with nails, pierced with a spear and mocked, giving His precious life for His friends. As she gazes on this, she feels the sword of love go through her heart, and she cries out:

“Stay me up with flowers, compass me about with fruits, for I languish with love.” The pomegranates that the Bride, led into her Beloved’s garden, loves to gather from the tree of life taste of the Bread of Heaven and have the colour of the Blood of Christ. She sees death struck its death blow, and the one who caused death made part of his Conqueror’s triumph. She sees the Victor rising in glory from hell to earth and from earth to heaven, followed by the crowd of the redeemed, so that at “the name of Jesus every knee may bow of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” Under the ancient curse, the earth was condemned to grow thorns and thistles. But now that God’s blessing has restored it, the Bride calls on it to cover her with flowers. Remembering the words, “My flesh hath flourished again, and with my will I will praise Him,” she renews her strength with the fruit of the tree of the cross and with the flowers of the Resurrection, whose heavenly fragrance draws the Beloved to visit her. Then He exclaims: “Behold thou art fair, my Beloved, and comely.” She shows how she longs for His coming and what her hope rests on: not on her own goodness, but on the sweetness of flowers gathered in a field the Lord has blessed. Such flowers are dear to the Christ who chose to be born and raised in Nazareth. The heavenly Bridegroom, drawn by the fragrance, loves to come into the room of the heart when He finds it hung with fruit and scented with flowers. He comes eagerly, and He loves to live in souls He sees are given to meditation, carefully gathering in the fruit of His Passion and the glorious flowers of His Resurrection. The precious crop that ripened through long ages of sin and death, and in these last days is ready to be gathered, is the harvest of the fruits of His Passion. But it is in the splendour of the Resurrection that the flowers bloom of the new springtime that grace has brought to the earth. At the end of time, at the general resurrection, the fruit will be beyond measure, “for winter is now past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers have appeared in our land.” By these words the Bride means: summer has come back with the One who broke up the ice of the old world to bring spring to everything, saying, “Behold I make all things new.” His body, sown in death, has blossomed in the resurrection, and in His likeness our plains and valleys, once dry and bare or frozen, are born again to life and warmth.

The freshness of these flowers, the ripeness of the fruit, and the beauty of this garden with its lovely scent also please the Father of the One who has made all things new. Blessing Him, the Father says: “Behold the smell of my Son is as the smell of a field full of flowers, which the Lord hath blessed;” full of flowers indeed, for it is from His fullness that we have all received. The Bride may come whenever she wishes, as one at home there, and gather flowers and fruit to decorate the room of her conscience, so that when the Bridegroom comes He finds the little bed of her heart filled with the sweetest scents. In the same way, if we want Christ to come to us and stay with us, we must fill our hearts with thoughts of His death and resurrection, and faithfully remember the mercy and the power He has shown us by them. This is what David meant when he said: “These two things have I heard: that power belongeth to God, and mercy to Thee, O Lord.” And Christ has proved it more than enough. He died to pay for our sins, He rose from the dead to make us right with God, and He sent the Holy Spirit to comfort us. One day He will return to complete our salvation. In His death we see the proof of His mercy, in His resurrection the proof of His power, and in the rest the proof of both together.

When the Bride begs to be held up with fragrant flowers and strengthened with sweet fruit, it is because she is afraid her love might cool or grow weak. But she needs such help only until she is brought into her Beloved’s room. Then she will feel Him covering her with the kisses she has longed for, and she will exclaim: “His left hand is under my head, and His right doth embrace me.” Then she will feel how far the embrace of His right hand surpasses every sweetness, and that the left hand, with which He held her in the first days of His coming, cannot compare with it. She will understand that “the flesh profiteth nothing; it is the Spirit that quickeneth.” She will grasp the meaning of His words: “My spirit is above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb.” When it is also written, “My memory is unto everlasting generations,” it is to show that the chosen ones who are not yet satisfied with the Bridegroom’s presence at least have His image to comfort them for as long as time lasts. When it is written, “They shall publish the memory of thine inexhaustible sweetness,” it clearly refers to those the Psalmist had just spoken of: “Generation and generation shall praise Thy works.” On earth we have only the memory of the Bridegroom; in heaven, His presence forever. That presence is the glory of those who have already reached harbour, and the memory is the comfort of those still battling the waves.

fields.title: Who Finds Comfort in God
fields.body_html:
IT is worth asking who it is that finds comfort in thinking about God. It is not the fallen people who keep provoking God, to whom it is said: “Woe, ye rich, unto you, for you have received your consolation.” It is those who can truly say: “My soul hath refused to be comforted.” Those who do not yet have the joy of the Beloved’s presence do well to fix their eyes on the future, and those who refuse to take anything from the stream of passing pleasures enjoy in hope, and in full measure, the joys that will last forever. These are the people who seek the face of the Lord, the God of Jacob, and not themselves. The thought of God is sweet to those who long for Him and bring His presence to mind with every breath. But instead of satisfying their hunger for Him, it makes them hungrier. He foretold this in the words, “They that eat Me shall yet hunger,” and the hungry one answers, “I shall be satisfied when Thy glory shall appear.” Yet even now, happy are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they alone will be filled. Woe to you, twisted and wicked generation; woe to you, foolish and blinded people, who do not love to think of Him but dread His coming. You have good reason to be afraid, because you will not escape the hunter’s net, for those who want to “become rich fall into the snares of the devil.” On that day you will not escape the terrible and hopeless sentence: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire.” But how sweet and tender is the promise we hear the Church repeat every day in remembrance of the Passion: “He that eateth My flesh and drinketh My blood hath everlasting life.” That means: whoever honours My death, and follows My example by putting the desires of the flesh to death on earth, will have eternal life; or, if you suffer with Me, you will also reign with Me. Even so, to this day, many who hear these words turn and go away sad, saying by their actions if not their lips: “This is a hard saying, who can bear it?” Those who would rather set their hearts on uncertain treasures than keep their hearts pure and stay faithful to God cannot bear any mention of the Cross. The very thought of the Passion seems unbearable to them. How will they bear the Judge’s sentence: “Go, ye cursed, into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels”? Those words will crush the ones they fall on like a huge rock. But the saints will be blessed. Like the Apostle, their only ambition is to “please God while absent from Him, and still to please Him when they shall be present.” They too will hear their sentence: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you.” On that day those who did not keep their hearts right will feel, too late, how sweet and light the yoke and burden of Christ was. In their hard-hearted pride they refused to carry it, as though it were a shameful and crushing weight. Poor slaves, you cannot toil for this world’s riches and also glory in the Cross of our Saviour Jesus Christ. You cannot want and work for earthly things and at the same time taste the sweetness of our Lord. One day you will certainly find Him terrifying, since thinking of Him has never been your joy.

But the believing soul longs for God with all her heart and lingers over the thought of Him. As long as she cannot see her Saviour face to face, she glories in the shame of the Cross. She is like Christ’s dove, sleeping and resting among the good things He has given her. Her wings are silver white with the purity and innocence that come, Lord Jesus, from longing for Your indescribable sweetness. And she hopes that in the glory shining from Your face her “feathers will shine like gold,” and that she will overflow with joy and be flooded with light from Your face in the delight of the saints. So she has good reason to say now with joy: “His left hand is under my head, and His right shall embrace me.” His left hand is the memory of that love, unmatched in its greatness, by which He laid down His life for those He loved. His right hand is the vision of Himself that He has promised His own, and the contentment with which He will fill and crown them when they enjoy His presence. The Psalms say: “At Thy right hand there are delights even to the end.” So His right hand rightly stands for the heavenly happiness, beyond all imagining, that comes from seeing God and makes us share in His life. In the same way, the left hand stands for that astonishing love I have spoken of, which we can never think about too much, for it is on this hand that the Bride lays her head and rests until this time of wickedness has passed. Her head can be taken to mean the aim of her soul, which she rests on her Bridegroom’s arm so that in her weakness she does not slip away to merely earthly attractions. For the earthly, perishable burden of the body weighs heavily on the soul and drags it down from higher thoughts. Yet she cannot fail to rise to them if she rests on the contemplation of such mercy, which she had so little right to expect: love so generous and so fully proved, gentleness and sweetness so patient and so fine, honour beyond imagining. How could these fail to lift up the mind that meditates on them, freeing it from every unworthy attachment, sinking ever deeper into it, and making it despise anything that cannot be enjoyed without giving up these higher joys? Their sweetness draws her like a rare perfume. She quickens her step gladly, and her heart is on fire with love. Knowing she is loved so tenderly makes her feel cold by comparison, though love is her very life. What return is it for so wonderful a love, coming down from so high, if a poor grain of dust is consumed with gratitude and love? Was it not the Majesty of heaven who loved first? Has He not shown Himself wholly given to the work of saving her? For “God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son.” This is clearly written of God the Father. And again: “He hath delivered His soul to death;” this is said of the Son. And of the Holy Spirit we read: “The Paraclete whom My Father will give you in My name, He will teach you all things, and will bring all things to your remembrance whatsoever I have said unto you.” From this we see that God loves us, and loves us with His whole being. The whole Blessed Trinity loves us, if we may dare to speak this way of the infinite, incomprehensible Being who is one and undivided.

fields.title: The Duty to Love God
fields.body_html:
EVERYTHING that has been said proves very clearly that we must love God and that He has a right to our love. What about the unbeliever? Since he does not know God the Son, he also does not know the Father or the Holy Spirit. And since he gives no glory to the Son, he does not glorify the Father who sent Him, or the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of both. He knows less of God than we do, so it is no surprise that he loves Him less. Still, he does know one thing: he owes himself entirely to the One who created him. But what about me? I cannot plead ignorance. I know that God made me without my deserving it, that He meets all my needs, comforts me with compassion, and guides me with tender care. More than that, I know that He is my Redeemer, the Author of my eternal salvation, my treasure and my glory. As it is written: “With Him is plentiful redemption;” “By His own blood He entered once into the Holy of Holies, having obtained eternal redemption.” He keeps us safe, as it is written: “The Lord knoweth the days of the undefiled, and their inheritance shall be for ever.” He makes us rich, as He has said: “Good measure, pressed down and shaken together and running over, shall they give into your bosom;” and elsewhere: “The eye hath not seen, O God, what things Thou hast prepared for them that wait for Thee.” He fills us with glory, as the Apostle says: “We wait for the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our body, now vile and abject, and make it like unto His own, which is full of glory.” And again: “The sufferings of this present time are not to be compared to the glory which shall be revealed in us.” And this present time of trouble in the world, so short and so fleeting, produces for us, if only we look past what is seen and fix our eyes on what is unseen, “an eternal and incomparable weight of glory.”

For all of this, what can I give back to the Lord? Both reason and the law of nature bind me to give myself wholly to the One from whom I have everything I have, and to devote my whole being to loving Him. And faith shows me that I am bound to love Him more than myself, the more I understand that I owe to His generosity not only everything I am, but also the gift of Himself.

But consider this. Before the day of Christian faith had dawned, before God had taken on our flesh and died on a cross, gone down into hell and ascended to the Father, that is, before the fullness of His love for us had shone out, long before all this, man had already been commanded to love the Lord his God with all his heart, with all his soul and with all his strength. That is, with his whole being, with all the love he is capable of as a creature given understanding and will. Could it be unfair of God to claim His own work and His own gifts for Himself? Why should the work not love the God who made it, since it has also been given the power to love? And why should it not love Him with all its powers, when it has those powers only from God? Consider also that man was not only called into being out of nothing, with no prior claim, but was called into being to be raised to high dignity. Then we will see even more clearly how bound we are to love Him wholly, and how right His claim on our love is. And when man had sunk to the level of the beasts that perish, did God not step in to restore and save him? Is that not the wonder of His goodness and His mercy? For by sin we had fallen from the dignity in which we were created and become like brutes, like the ox that eats grass and has no light of reason. If I owe my whole self to my Creator, what do I not owe to my Redeemer, and to such a Redeemer! Creating was a far smaller work than redeeming. God had only to speak the word and all things were made. But to repair the fall of what one word had created, what wonders He had to perform, what cruelties, and even what humiliations, He had to suffer!

What, then, shall I give back to the Lord for all He has done for me? By creating me, He gave me to myself. But He gave me back to myself when He gave Himself to me. Given first and then restored, I owe myself to Him twice over. But what do I owe God for the gift of Himself? If I gave Him my whole being a thousand times over, what would that be compared with God?

fields.title: A Summary
fields.body_html: I ADMIT that God deserves to be greatly loved, or rather that He should be loved beyond all measure. He loved first: He so great, we so small. He loves us to excess, just as we are, with no claim at all on our side. That is why the right measure of our love for God is to go beyond all measure. Since God, the one we love, is infinite, how can we weigh or measure the love we owe Him? Besides, our love is not a free gift; it is the payment of a debt. And since the One who loves us is the I Am, eternal and boundless, Divine Love, God, whose greatness has no limits and whose wisdom has no bounds, the “Peace which passeth all understanding,” since it is such a God who loves us, how could we say we will love Him this much and no more? “I will love Thee, O Lord, my strength and my defence, my refuge and my salvation,” You who are everything my soul needs and everything my heart desires. My God and my Help, I will love You with all my strength, not as much as You deserve, but as much as my small capacity allows. I will love You more when You have given me more power to love, but never, never as You ought to be loved. Your eyes see my foolishness and my weakness, but I know that You write in Your book those who do what they can, even when they cannot do what they ought. Have I not said enough to show how God should be loved, and by what gifts He has earned our love? I only name His gifts, because who could express, understand or even feel how great they are?

fields.title: The Reward of Loving God
fields.body_html:
LET us look at what good comes to us from loving God. Even if we see it very imperfectly, that is better than not seeing it at all. We have spoken, in a way unworthy of God but as well as we could, of His right to our love. Now we will speak of the reward He has attached to our loving Him. For although we must love God without any thought of reward, we will still be rewarded for having loved Him. True love cannot go unpaid, even though it is not in it for the pay and does not seek its own. Love is the soul going out toward someone, not a contract. It does not come from a bargain and cannot be bought by agreement. It moves freely, and it makes us like itself. True love is its own satisfaction. Its reward is the one it loves.

For whatever we seem to love, if what we really want is something else, then it is that something else we love, and not the thing our heart uses to reach it. St. Paul did not preach the gospel to earn his daily bread; the bread that kept him alive let him preach the gospel. What he loved was the gospel, not the bread. True love does not look for a reward, but it earns one. Certainly no one offers to pay for love, yet love not only deserves its reward but will surely receive it. Even in lower things, who are the people who need to be stirred by the offer of rewards? Those who are lazy and have no love for the work. Does anyone ever think of offering pay to persuade people who are longing to be allowed to serve? No one gives money to a starving man to get him to eat, or to a loving mother to get her to nurse her child, or to a vinedresser to get him to look after his vines, or to a homeowner to get him to rebuild his fallen house. Far less does the one who loves God need to be urged on by the promise of any reward other than God Himself. Otherwise it would be the reward he loved, not God.

It is natural for a reasoning being to want whatever seems to him, by his own way of thinking, better than what he has, and never to be satisfied if something good lacks the particular quality he prefers. If he loves beauty, he will want whatever seems most beautiful to him. If he is proud of owning a very precious jewel, he will want one even more splendid. However rich he is, his nature is to want more. Do we not see it every day? The owner of huge property and wealth keeps buying more land and is never content unless he is expanding his estates. Do those who live in vast palaces not keep building new ones, always remodelling, making the square round and the round square? Do people in high positions not keep reaching for higher ones, always climbing, driven by an ambition that grows harder and harder to satisfy? There is no end to this restlessness, because in such things it is impossible to reach a point that is perfectly good and high. And it is not surprising that as long as someone can see something greater and better beyond him, he is dissatisfied with having what is smaller and worse. What does seem foolish beyond words is to keep longing for things that cannot even quiet our desires, let alone satisfy them. What follows? The heart, tempted by many deceptive charms, wears itself out for nothing. It is always craving, counts what it has enjoyed as nothing compared with what it would like to have, and is so tormented by wanting what it does not have that it takes no pleasure in what it does have. No one can have everything. Even the little one can get must be paid for with hard work, and enjoyed with anxiety, indeed with the miserable certainty that one day it will be lost, though no one knows when that day will be.

I have described how a twisted will behaves as it blindly searches for the highest good. It rushes about in vain, the plaything of its own emptiness, deceived by wickedness. Why waste the day struggling uselessly this way and that, only to be overtaken by death unsatisfied? This is the trap the worldly fall into when they hunt about like fools for what their souls desire. They use up their lives in useless effort and never reach perfect happiness, because they love created things and not the Creator. They try one thing and then another before it ever occurs to them to try the Lord who made them all. Yet if they could have everything their hearts desire and own the whole world without its Maker, they would finally feel, by the same law that has ruled their whole life, that they must have Him or never rest. They have moved from one ambition to the next, always wanting something better. Now, as masters of everything in heaven and earth, they would soon find it all not enough, and discover that they must seek the One who is still missing. They must seek God Himself.

Once they discover that and reach Him, there is peace, because there is nowhere further to go. The soul is bound to cry out: “It is good for me to adhere to my God;” or, “What besides Thee have I in heaven, and besides Thee what do I desire upon earth?” and again: “Thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever.” A soul would end up in God even by that route, if it could try every lesser thing in turn. But life is too short, strength would give out long before, and there are too many rivals. It would be impossible to try every created thing and find it lacking. It is easier and more profitable to do the testing in our minds than in real life. Our minds were given more energy and sharper sight than our hearts for exactly this purpose: so that they can go ahead and keep the heart from attaching itself to anything the mind has not first judged worth desiring. “Prove all things: hold fast that which is good.” The mind should prepare the ground for the heart, so that the heart follows the mind’s judgment. Otherwise there is no hope of “ascending into the mountain of the Lord, and dwelling in His holy place.” It is useless to have a reasoning mind if we act like animals and simply obey our senses, with reason having no say. Those who are not guided by reason do run the race, but they run with no chance of winning.

How could they win, when they do not put the prize first, but last of all? How could they do anything except lose themselves in a maze with no beginning or end? It is not like that for the just. Warned by the blame laid on those who go astray in this way (for the road to death is wide and well trodden), they choose the king’s highway, which turns neither right nor left, for “the path of the just is straight.” They take the shortest road, guided by a word that is simple and makes everything simple: not to be taken in by what their eyes see, but to sell everything and give to the poor. Blessed indeed are such poor, for the kingdom of heaven is theirs. The Lord knows the way of the just and approves it. He also knows the way of the sinner, where the sinner is bound to perish. The just are happy in their poverty, and the rich are unsatisfied in their plenty, for the wise man says: “He that loveth riches shall reap no fruit from them.” But those who “hunger and thirst after justice shall be filled.” Justice is the food they need. The things of this world no more feed the soul than air feeds the body. If we saw a starving man gulping air with his mouth wide open, drinking long drafts of wind to quench his thirst, we would say, “Poor fool!” It is the same with those who try to satisfy the soul with worldly goods. These only puff it up like wind; they no more feed it than spiritual things feed our bodies. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who satisfieth thy desire with good things.” He fills you from His fullness, at once giving you what you desire and stirring you to want more. He goes before you, He holds you up, He fills you. He lights desire in your heart, and He Himself is what all desire is for.

I have said that the reason for our love of God is God Himself, and that is rightly said, because He is both the source and the goal of our love. He is such that it is impossible to know Him and not love Him, or not hope in Him. For if we did not hope to love Him perfectly in the life to come, our love for Him now would be nothing. His love prepares our love and rewards it. In His great goodness He loves us first. Then He asks for the love that is due to Him, and allows us the most glorious hopes for the future. He is generous to those who call on Him, but He can give nothing better than Himself. He Himself is the goal of all our striving and our reward. He is the food of holy souls and the ransom of those still held captive. If the Lord is good to the soul that seeks Him, what is He to the soul that has found Him? Yet this may seem strange: no one can seek the Lord who has not already found Him. For He wills to be found so that He may be sought still more, and to be sought so that He may be found more completely. But although He can be sought and found, He can never be beaten to it. He is always first. Even if we say, “In the morning my prayer shall prevent Thee,” it is still quite certain that our prayer would be very cold, O God, if Your inspiration did not come before it.

We have spoken of where the love of God ends; now let us look at how it begins.

fields.title: The First Degree of Love
fields.body_html:
LOVE is one of the four natural feelings that everyone knows, so there is no need to list them. Now, it is only natural and right to love the Author of nature first of all, and the first and greatest commandment is: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God.” But nature is too soft and weak for such a command. It has to begin by loving itself. This is the love called carnal, by which a person loves himself first and above all, as it is written: “That is not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural.” We love first by nature, not because we are told to. “No man ever hated his own flesh.” But if this love grows too strong, if like a river it overflows its banks and floods the land around, it turns into self-indulgence. Against that flood this dyke is set: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” It is only fair that the one who shares our nature should share our love. So if anyone cannot love his brothers and sisters enough to think of their needs, or let us even say their pleasures, let him go without those very things himself, so that he may learn. A person may think of himself as much as he likes, as long as he takes care to think just as much of his neighbour. This, friend, is the curb and the fair limit set on you by the law of your being and by your conscience, so that your selfishness does not carry you away to your ruin and leave your nature at the mercy of your soul’s enemies, that is, your passions. It is far better to share with your neighbours than with your enemies. If, as the wise man advises, a person turns away from his passions, is content with food and clothing, and is willing to hold back his love for the things of the flesh that war against the spirit, I think he will find it easy to give his neighbour what he refuses to the enemy of his soul. His love will stay within the bounds of fairness and moderation from the moment he gives his brothers and sisters what he denies himself. Self-love becomes kindness by widening its circle.

But what if, by giving to our neighbour, we end up in need ourselves? What can we do then? Pray. We have only to pray with confidence to the One who gives all things generously and without reproach, who “openeth His hand and filleth with blessing every living creature.” We cannot doubt that He who gives most people more than they need will gladly give the one who prays for what he cannot do without. For it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and His justice, and all these things shall be added unto you.” By this God binds Himself to provide what is essential for the one who denies himself and loves his neighbour. To take on the yoke of purity and self-control rather than be a slave to our passions is to seek first the kingdom of God and to ask His help against the tyranny of sin. And it is only just to share our natural blessings with those who share our nature. But for our love of our neighbour to be wholly right, God must have His part in it. We cannot love our neighbour as we should except in God, and whoever does not love God cannot love anything in Him. So we must begin by loving God, and then love our neighbour in Him. God is the author of our love for Him, as He is of everything else. More than that, just as He created nature, He also keeps it going, for nature could neither come into being nor continue without Him. So that we would know this thoroughly and not take credit for anything ourselves, God, in the depths of His wisdom and love, allowed us to face trouble. Weak and needy as we are, we are driven to turn to God, and when He rescues us we give glory to His name. These are His own words: “Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me.” In this way a person who by nature is earthly and fleshly, with no love but for himself, is led through self-love to love God. He comes to see that whatever strength he has, at least for doing good, comes from God, and that without Him he can do nothing.

fields.title: The Second and Third Degrees of Love
fields.body_html: SO at first a person loves God for his own sake, not for God’s. Even that is something: to feel the limits of his own strength, to know what he cannot do without God’s help, and to stay on good terms with the One who keeps him alive and strong. But suppose a run of troubles comes and forces him to turn to God again and again, and each time he receives the help he needs. His heart would have to be made of brass or marble not to be moved in the end by the goodness of his Helper, and not to begin at last to love Him for Himself. When frequent trials bring us often to God’s feet, we cannot help beginning to know Him, and knowing Him, we come to taste His sweetness. Soon we are brought to love Him rightly, far more for the sweetness and beauty we find in Him than for our own advantage. As the Samaritans said to the woman: “We now believe, not for thy saying; for we ourselves have heard Him, and know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world.” In the same way, we come to say to our natural self: “It is not because of you that we love the Lord. We have tasted for ourselves and found how sweet He is.” The needs of this life become a kind of language, proclaiming with joy and thanksgiving the blessings whose value they have taught us. Once this has been learned, it is easy enough to obey the command to love our neighbour as ourselves. For if we truly love God, we love everything that is His, and from then on it is easy to follow the command: “Purify your hearts in the obedience of charity, with a brotherly love.” We are bound to keep so fair a command willingly, a command that is also so rewarding precisely because it is unselfish. It is a most pure love, because it shows itself simply in holy actions and in truth. It is most just, because it gives back what it receives. Whoever loves with this love loves as he is loved, and no longer seeks his own interests but the things of Jesus Christ, just as Jesus Christ sought ours. Here we see the love that said, “Give praise to the Lord, for He is good.” Whoever loves God because He is good, not good to him but good in Himself, truly loves God for God’s sake. He is not like the one of whom Scripture says, “He will praise Thee when Thou shalt do well to him.”

fields.title: The Fourth Degree of Love
fields.body_html:
HAPPY is the one who can rise to the fourth degree of love, and loves himself only for God’s sake. “Thy justice, O Lord, is as the high mountains.” So it is with this fourth degree of love, “a great mountain in which God is well pleased to dwell.” “Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord?” “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly thither and be at rest?” “His place is in peace, and his abode in Zion.” “Woe is me that my sojourning is prolonged.” When will this flesh and blood, this dust and mud I am made of, be able to climb up there? When will my soul, carried away with love for God, see herself as a broken pot, long for God, and lose herself in Him, for “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit”? When will she cry out: “My flesh and my heart have fainted away; Thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever”? Holy and happy is the one who has felt something like this even once, for a single moment, in this mortal life. For this is no human happiness. To lose oneself like this, as if empty of self, as if one did not exist, is eternal life. If some poor mortal reaches it for a moment, almost without noticing, this evil age seems to resent it, delaying and spoiling his joy. This body of death drags him down. The cares and worries of life pull him back. The weakness of the flesh will not support him. And his duty to his neighbour loudly calls him to come back down, so that he cries out: “Lord, I suffer violence, answer Thou for me;” or: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”

We read in Holy Scripture that God has made all things for Himself. So His creatures are bound to shape themselves, at least in some measure, to the mind of their Maker. We should offer ourselves to Him completely, seeking only what pleases Him, not what pleases us. We will find happiness far less in pursuing our own advantage than in His will being done in us, as we pray every day: “Thy will be done on earth as it is in Heaven.” O pure and holy love! Most sweet and blessed affection! O complete surrender of an unselfish soul, most perfect because there is no thought of self in it, most sweet and tender because everything the soul feels is from God!

To reach this is for the soul to be made like God. A small drop of water seems to disappear when it is mixed with wine, taking on its taste and colour. A bar of iron plunged into a furnace seems to lose its own nature and take on the nature of fire. Air filled with sunlight seems to become light itself rather than simply being lit up. It is the same with the natural life of the saints: they seem to melt and pass into the will of God. For if anything merely human were left in us, how could God be all in all? It is not that human nature will be destroyed, but that it will gain a different beauty, a higher power and glory. When will that be? Who will be allowed to see and know it? When shall I come and appear before the face of God? O God, my Lord, my heart has said to You: “My face hath sought Thee; Thy face, O Lord, will I seek.” Will someone like me be allowed to see Your holy temple?

In this life the heart has to give some thought to the body, and the mind has to make sure its health and strength are kept up. I believe that as long as our energies are divided like this, it is impossible to rest wholly in God and in contemplating Him, and impossible to keep perfectly the command, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy soul, and with all thy strength.” We cannot hope to possess the fourth degree of love, or rather to be possessed by it, until we have put on a spiritual and immortal body, pure and at peace, obedient and in every way subject to the spirit. That cannot be our doing; it can only be the work of God’s power for those who please Him. Our soul will easily reach this perfect love when neither the weight nor the temptations of this body press on her. Then she will leap, unhindered, into her joy in the Lord. But should we doubt that the souls of the holy martyrs tasted this happiness, at least a little, before they left their triumphant bodies? This much we know for certain: an immense love filled them and carried them away, giving them strength to lay down their lives and endure the tortures they suffered. Even so, the joy of their triumph must have been lessened by that pain.

fields.title: Perfect Love After the Resurrection
fields.body_html:
WHAT, then, can we believe about souls already set free from the burden of the flesh? I believe they are completely immersed in the bottomless depths of eternal light, in an eternity full of light. But if, as we cannot deny, they still long and hope to be reunited with the bodies they once lived in, then clearly they have not been completely changed. Their bodies still have some claim on them, however small. Until death is wholly swallowed up in victory, until the glory of eternity has filled every corner of the realm of night, and the brightness of heavenly light shines even in our bodies, our souls can never throw themselves wholly into God and give themselves entirely to Him. Until then the chains of the body still hold them back, if only through a natural affection they have neither the will nor the power to give up. Until our bodies are restored, our souls can never be swallowed up in God, which is their complete perfection. If union with Him could be completed by the soul alone, she would no longer want the body. But when the soul leaves the body it is gain, and it is greater gain when she is reunited with it. Finally, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints.” If death can be praised like that, what will life be, that life! The soul may well expect to gain more glory from her body, because, weak and mortal as it is, it has added greatly to her merits. “To them that love God all things work together unto good;” and the soul that loves God gains from her poor, weak body whether it is living, dead or risen. While it lives, it bears the fruits of repentance with her. When it dies, it rests from its labour. When it rises, the two together reach the fullness of all joy. So it is clear that without the body the soul is not made perfect, since in every state the body is essential to her good.

The body, then, is a faithful companion for the soul. If it is a burden, it is also a help. When it stops helping, it also stops hindering. And when it helps again, it is no longer a burden. The first state is hard work but profitable. The second is inactive but in no way tiresome. And the third is glorious. Listen to how the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs invites the soul to these three states: “Eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved.” The souls He invites to eat are those still labouring in their bodies. Those resting in death He urges to drink. Those clothed in their bodies once more He invites to be filled to overflowing. By calling these His dearly beloved, He shows that they are full of love. To the first He says only “friends,” for those still labouring under the weight of the body are dear to Him in proportion to the love they have. Those set free from the burden of the flesh are dearer still, because of the freedom and fullness their love has gained. But most dearly loved of all are those who, clothed again in the robe of the glorious body, are carried away by the love of God in joyful freedom from everything that could drag them down or hinder their upward flight. Only when they are made perfect like this are they truly free. In the first state the body tires the spirit and holds it back. In the second, the body is something hoped for and personally longed for, and that longing still has a trace of self in it. The faithful soul begins by eating bread, but, sadly, “in the sweat of her face.” For as long as she is in the body she walks by faith, and faith must work through love, since faith without works is dead. These works are her bread, as the Lord said: “My bread is to do the will of my Father.” When she has laid aside the body of death, she stops eating the bread of sorrow, and, as at the end of a meal, she drinks long drafts of the wine of love. But this wine is not yet pure, for as the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs, “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” With the wine of God’s love the soul mixes milk, that is, the desire to be reunited with her body, which she loves with the tenderness of natural affection. She already feels the strength of the divine love she is drinking, but it does not yet carry her away; the milk mixed with it still softens it. Being carried away like that unsettles the spirit so that it forgets itself. But that is not the state of a soul still longing for her body, which has yet to rise. She does not wholly lose the sense of self. Yet once she has regained the one thing she lacks, what is there to stop her throwing herself completely into God, losing even her own likeness as she is made like Him? With nothing left in the way, she can raise to her lips the cup of wisdom of which it is written: “My chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it.” Who could be surprised that she is carried away by the abundance that fills the house of God? Free from every care, in the Kingdom of the Father, she drinks long, peaceful drafts of the Son’s wine, pure and new.

It is wisdom that gives this threefold banquet, where all the food is love. She gives bread to those who still have work to do, wine to drink for those who already enjoy rest, and fills to overflowing those who have entered the kingdom of heaven. When her guests have eaten, she serves them wine. As long as we labour in this life, carrying a mortal body, we must eat the bread our work has earned us; we must eat it with effort and swallow it down. But as soon as we have breathed our last, we begin to drink in our spiritual life, receiving the cup and drinking in happy rest. When all is complete, and the body is raised to life and given back to the soul, they drink their fill from the cup that never runs dry. This is the meaning of the words: “Eat, O my friends, and drink; and be inebriated, my dearly beloved.” In this life, eat. After death you will drink. In the kingdom of the resurrection you will be filled to overflowing, you whom I may rightly call My dearly beloved. Are they not truly beloved who are admitted to the wedding feast of the Lamb, who sit at His table, eating and drinking in His kingdom, when “He presents to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing”? Then He will fill His dearly beloved to overflowing, pouring out for them a “torrent of delights.” For when the Bridegroom holds the Bride in His loving and pure embrace, a torrent of delight will gladden the City of God. By that torrent I understand none other than the Son of God, who “passing, will minister unto them that sit at meat.” So He has promised that the just will feast and rejoice before God and be delighted with gladness. From this comes a fullness that never grows tired, a longing that is never quenched yet is completely calm and at peace, an eternal desire to possess that comes from no lack, and a joy that overflows without excess, coming not from wine but from God and His Truth. The soul has reached the fourth degree of love forever when she loves only God and loves Him above all, when she loves for no gain but for Him alone. Then He Himself is her reward, the eternal reward of those who love Him and will love Him forever.
